parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones an optician's to book an eye test.
script: Good morning, Clearview Opticians, Mia speaking. How can I help you?
Oh, hello. I'd like to book an eye test, please. I haven't had one for about three years, so I'm probably overdue.
That's no problem at all. Is this your first time with us?
It is, yes. I've just moved to the area.
Welcome, then. I'll take a few details first. Can I have your surname, please?
Could you spell that for me?
Thank you, Mr Whitcombe. And your postcode?
It's LS6 2PD. No, sorry, I've got that wrong. It's LS6 2PT. I keep writing the old one from my last flat.
LS6 2PT. Lovely. I've already got your phone number from the screen, so we're fine there. Now, which day would suit you? We have space on Tuesday and Wednesday next week.
Hmm. I'm working in the mornings, I'm afraid, so it would have to be the afternoon. Do you have anything on Tuesday afternoon?
Let me see. No, Tuesday afternoon is completely full. Wednesday afternoon I can do you at 2.30, or at 4.15.
Wednesday's fine. If I could have 4.15, that would be perfect, because I can leave work a bit early.
Right, Wednesday at 4.15. Now, it helps the optometrist if I know why you're coming in. Is it just a routine check, or have you noticed any problems?

Well, it's mainly the headaches, to be honest. I get quite bad ones in the evenings, usually after I've been staring at a computer all day. My eyes get tired and the words on the screen look a bit blurred sometimes too, but it's the headaches that really bother me.
That's very common these days. I'll put that on your record. Do you wear contact lenses at all?
No, only glasses, and I've had the same pair for about four years. They're getting scratched.
I see. And is there any history of eye conditions in your family?
My mother has glaucoma, actually. Is that something I should mention?
Definitely. I'll make a note of it so the optometrist can check your eye pressure. You'll be seeing Ms Adeyemi. That's A-D-E-Y-E-M-I. She's very thorough, and she's good at explaining things.
Great. And how much will the test cost?
The standard eye test is 25 pounds. We also offer an extended test with a retinal scan, which is 40 pounds, but you only need that if the optometrist recommends it.
No, I'll stick with the standard one, thank you.
Of course. The test takes about forty minutes. If you do need glasses, you can look at frames straight afterwards. Do you know what kind of style you'd like?
I've had square frames for years and I'm a bit tired of them, to be honest. I think I'd like round ones this time, and something fairly light.

We've got a good range of those. Now, since you spend so much time at a computer, the optometrist may suggest a special coating on the lenses. It's designed to reduce glare from screens. Some people ask about a blue light filter instead, but the evidence for that is a bit mixed, so we normally recommend the other one.
OK, I'll see what she says. Is there anything I need to bring with me?
Yes, please bring a list of any medication you're taking, because some tablets can affect your eyes. And do bring the glasses you're wearing now, although I expect you'd have done that anyway.
Right. I'll write the medication down so I don't forget.
Perfect. If you need new lenses, they're normally ready in about a week, and we'll text you when they arrive. We're on Park Lane, opposite the library, and there's free parking behind the building.
That's really helpful. Thank you very much for your help.
You're welcome, Mr Whitcombe. See you on Wednesday at 4.15. Goodbye.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: The manager of an open-air swimming pool introduces the coming season.
script: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming to the preview morning at Fernbank Open-Air Pool. I'm Dale, the pool manager, and over the next few minutes I'll tell you what's new for the coming season, and what's not quite ready yet.

Let's start with the dates. Those of you who've been coming for years will remember that we've always opened on the first of May, and the leaflet in your hand still says that, because it was printed before the problems started. The resurfacing of the pool surround has taken longer than we planned, so this year we'll open on the fifteenth of May instead. After that we'll stay open every day until the last Sunday in September, as usual.

The biggest change this year is the water. Until now we've heated it with old gas boilers, and on a cool morning it could feel pretty bracing. Over the winter we installed a heat pump, so the water will now be kept at around twenty-six degrees. That's about two degrees warmer than last summer, and it uses much less energy. We did discuss replacing the changing rooms, and we did get quotes, and I know they're showing their age, but the heating was the priority, so the changing rooms will get their turn next year. And before anyone asks, no, there's no new cafe. The old kiosk stays, although it will be selling hot drinks a bit earlier in the morning.

Now, season tickets. The price is going up slightly, from 120 pounds to 125 pounds, which I think is still good value. The real benefit for season ticket holders is that you can swim before we open to the general public, from half past six until half past eight, when the lanes are quiet. We did think about letting each ticket holder bring a free guest, but we decided that would make the pool too crowded at weekends. And you don't need to book a lane. It's first come, first served, as it always has been.

Now for some disappointing news. The high diving board will be out of use when we open. It passed its safety inspection in March, and all of our lifeguards are trained to supervise it. The problem is a replacement spring mechanism, which we ordered from Germany. It hasn't arrived, and the supplier is saying not before July. As soon as it comes, we'll fit it, and we'll put a notice on the website.

You may have noticed, too, that the main car park is being resurfaced as well, and the council has started road works on Elm Road, which isn't helping. The good news is that Fernbank Primary School, next door, has agreed to let us use its car park at weekends, so there will be about eighty extra spaces on Saturdays and Sundays. We'd still encourage you to cycle if you can. There's a new bike shelter by the entrance, and it's free to use.

Right, now let me run through the weekly timetable, which is on the back of the leaflet. The general public sessions run all day, every day, but we've also got some special sessions, and I'll go through them one by one.

If you're interested in exercise, aqua fitness classes will be on Wednesday evenings. We tried Thursdays last year, but a lot of people said they had other commitments, so we've moved it. The classes last forty-five minutes and are suitable for all abilities.

For the youngest swimmers, we're running lessons for children under five on Saturday mornings. Those fill up quickly, so please book as soon as you can at reception. Older children have lessons on weekdays after school, and I'll give you the details afterwards.
On Sundays we're holding what we call the family fun afternoon, with inflatables in the pool, and everyone is welcome. It's very popular, so arrive early if you want a space on the grass.

On Friday evenings we're trying something new: an evening swim with music, from seven until nine. We'll be playing the sort of songs you can sing along to, so I hope you'll join us and, if you're feeling brave, sing along.

Finally, on Monday mornings we'll have a quiet session for the over-sixties. The pool will be kept calm, with no splashing games, and there'll be tea and biscuits afterwards. We tried this on Tuesdays in the past, but Monday suits the local seniors' club better.

That's everything from me. If you have any questions, please come and find me by the kiosk, and I'll be happy to help. Enjoy the rest of your morning, and I look forward to seeing you in the water in May.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students discuss their sociology project on volunteering.
script: Hi, Owen. Did you get my message about the sociology project?
I did. I've been looking through the notes from last week, and I think we're finally getting somewhere.
Me too. Shall we go over where we've got to before we meet Dr Okonkwo on Friday?
Good idea. Well, first of all, I'm still glad we chose volunteering. Dr Okonkwo did suggest something about community health, remember, but it was my summer at the food bank that gave us the idea.
Yes, and that article I found about falling numbers of volunteers helped us justify it. But you're right, it was really your experience that made the decision.
Right. And I think changing our research question was the best thing we did.
Definitely. At first we wanted to know why people start volunteering, but there's so much research on that already.
Exactly. So now we're asking why they stop, which nobody seems to have looked at in our area. That's much more interesting.
And much more useful for the organisations, as well. Now, the questionnaire. I know we ran that pilot, and I was a bit worried about it.
Well, we got plenty of replies, more than enough, really. The trouble was that it was far too long. Forty questions, and loads of people left the open questions blank.
I know. I think they got bored by the middle. Ethics approval came through quickly, at least, so that wasn't a problem. That's why we decided to do interviews instead.
Yes. So far we've done twelve, and we plan to do about eight more.
Have you noticed anything about the people we've spoken to?
Only that nearly all of them are over fifty. We really need to find some younger volunteers, otherwise the results will be biased.
True. I could ask at the student union, perhaps. Anyway, shall we go through what each organisation told us? We can start with the food bank.
Yes. Everyone there kept saying how close they all are. One woman called it her second family. There are a lot of retired people there, but that's not unusual.
No. The animal shelter was quite different, wasn't it? Several volunteers said people leave within about three months.
That's right. The hours are flexible, but the work is emotionally hard, and they said that's the main reason people stop. It has a really high turnover.
Then there was the hospital visiting scheme. I was impressed by how well prepared they felt.
Yes, they all did a three-day course before they started, and nearly everyone mentioned it. They said it gave them confidence. I think that's why most of them stay.
The river clean-up group was interesting too. They never put up posters or anything like that.
No, they recruit almost entirely through social media. Someone posts a photo of a clean stretch of riverbank, and people just turn up the next weekend.
And finally the youth football club. That was the one that surprised me.
Me too. The coaches were friendly enough, but several of them said that nobody ever thanked them. The parents just take it for granted that they'll be there.
Which is probably something we should highlight in our report. Now, what do you want to ask Dr Okonkwo on Friday?
I thought about asking for an extension, but honestly we're on track, so there's no need. And the consent forms are all signed.
So what's left? I'm still not sure how to present the numbers from the interviews.
That's it, then. We'll ask her how to present the statistics. Whether to use graphs or tables, and how much to say about such a small sample.
Good. And I'll start drafting the introduction tonight, if you can look at the methods section.
Fine. Let's meet again on Thursday to put it all together.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about glaciers as records of past climates.
script: Good afternoon. In today's lecture I want to look at glaciers, not as scenery or as a source of fresh water, but as archives. A glacier is a kind of library of past climates, and the more carefully we learn to read it, the more we discover about how our planet has changed.

Let me begin with how a glacier forms. A glacier appears in places where more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Year after year, the snow that survives piles up, and the weight of the upper layers compresses the lower ones, squeezing out most of the air and turning the snow first into a granular material called firn, and eventually into dense ice. This can take a few decades in a warm, wet place, or many thousands of years in the cold, dry interior of Antarctica.

Now, the crucial point is that as the snow is compressed, not all of the air escapes. Tiny bubbles remain sealed inside the ice, and each bubble holds a small sample of the atmosphere as it was when that snow fell. So when we drill out a core of ice, we are, in effect, holding ancient air in our hands.

An ice core is a long cylinder, typically about ten centimetres across, drilled out with a hollow drill and stored at minus thirty degrees. The longest continuous core from Antarctica, drilled on the high plateau, goes back around 800,000 years. Cores from Greenland are shorter, at about a hundred thousand years, but they have more detail, because more snow falls there.

That brings me to the layers. In places with distinct seasons, each year leaves a visible band: summer snow is coarser and darker than winter snow, rather like the rings of a tree. The thickness of each annual layer tells us how much snow fell in that year, so we can reconstruct changes in precipitation, and not only in temperature.

The layers also contain impurities. Some contain dust blown from deserts, which tells us about wind and dryness. But for dating, the most useful impurity is volcanic ash. A big eruption leaves a thin layer that can be found in cores from all over the world, and if we know the date of that eruption from historical records, we can use the layer as a marker to check our counting.

Now, how do we measure past temperatures? The water in the ice contains two forms of oxygen, a heavier one and a lighter one. In cold periods, less of the heavier form reaches the poles, so the ratio between the two acts like a thermometer, and gives us temperatures for each layer, going back through many ice ages.

Then there are the bubbles themselves. When we analyse the air inside them, we find that levels of carbon dioxide have risen and fallen in step with temperature through eight ice age cycles. And the present level is higher than at any time in the whole record. That is probably the single most important result to come out of ice core research.

Of course, polar ice is not the only archive. High in the Andes, tropical glaciers also preserve records. There's no real winter there, so the layers are harder to count, but they have a different story to tell. They record periods of severe drought, because dust blown from dried-up lakes builds up in thick dark bands. Some researchers think they may also show the effects of El Nino, though that is still being debated.

Even the retreat of a glacier is informative. As a glacier advances, it pushes rock and gravel ahead of it, and when it melts back, it leaves ridges of this debris at its edge. These ridges are called moraines, and their position shows how far the glacier once extended, which we can then date. And in Alaska, as the ice has retreated, it has uncovered tree stumps that are still rooted in the ground. Dating these stumps has shown that the land was once covered by forest, which tells us it was much warmer there some thousands of years ago.

I should end with a warning. Many of the world's glaciers are now shrinking so quickly that their records are disappearing before we can read them. In some mountain ranges, scientists are racing to drill cores and store them in freezers, so that future generations can analyse them with better techniques. We are, in a sense, rescuing the books from a library that is slowly melting. Thank you.

passages.title: From precious metal to drinks can: the story of aluminium
paras: A  Today aluminium is so ordinary that most of us throw it away without a second thought. A drinks can weighs less than a handful of coins and costs a fraction of a penny to make. Yet for much of the nineteenth century the metal was among the most valuable substances in the world. Aluminium is the most abundant metallic element in the Earth's crust, making up about eight per cent of it by weight, but it is never found on its own. It is locked inside compounds, mostly clays and a rock called bauxite, and the chemical bonds are so strong that the ordinary smelting which had served for iron and copper for thousands of years simply cannot break them. For centuries, therefore, people walked on, built with and ploughed through the stuff without any idea that a useful metal lay inside it.

B  The first person to isolate aluminium was probably the Danish scientist Hans Christian Ørsted, who in 1825 produced a small, impure lump of it. Two years later the German chemist Friedrich Wöhler repeated the experiment and obtained a grey powder, and by 1845 he had made pieces of metal about the size of pinheads. The breakthrough towards manufacture came in 1854, when the French chemist Henri Sainte-Claire Deville developed a method that used sodium to draw aluminium out of its compounds. Sodium was itself costly, so the process remained expensive, and a kilogram of aluminium still cost more than a kilogram of silver. Deville's small factory near Paris produced only a few tonnes in its first years, hardly enough to make the metal a part of everyday life.

C  Rarity gave the metal glamour. The French emperor Napoleon III, who had helped to pay for Deville's research, was fascinated by its lightness and by the idea of equipping his soldiers with aluminium armour. According to a famous story, at one banquet he reserved the aluminium plates and cutlery for his most honoured guests, while lesser visitors had to make do with gold. Jewellers made bracelets and ornaments from it. In 1884 the builders of the Washington Monument in the United States topped the tower with a small aluminium pyramid, chosen because the metal conducts electricity well and does not stain, even though it cost as much as silver. At the time it was the largest single piece of aluminium ever cast.

D  Everything changed in 1886, when two young men working independently on opposite sides of the Atlantic, Charles Martin Hall in Ohio and Paul Héroult in France, hit on the same idea within weeks of each other. They dissolved aluminium oxide in molten cryolite, a mineral, and passed a strong electric current through the mixture. Pure aluminium collected at the bottom of the vessel. Two years later the Austrian chemist Karl Josef Bayer devised a cheap way of extracting the oxide from bauxite. The two processes, which are still the basis of production today, made it possible to produce the metal in quantity, and within a few decades its price had fallen to a tiny fraction of what it had been.

E  The new method had a huge appetite for electricity, however, and smelters were therefore built beside hydroelectric power stations, in places such as Niagara Falls, the Norwegian fjords and the Scottish Highlands. Demand grew as engineers discovered what a light and strong metal could do. The frames of airships, and then of aircraft, were made from aluminium alloys, and the Second World War turned the metal into a strategic material: thousands of bombers were built from it. When peace returned, producers were left with enormous surplus capacity, and had to find new customers. They found them in kitchens, in window frames, in cars and in food packaging, from foil to trays.

F  The drinks can was one of the most successful of these new markets. Early cans were made of steel, which was heavy and prone to rust. The first aluminium cans appeared in the late 1950s, and brewers and soft-drink makers soon appreciated that they were lighter to transport, cooled more quickly in a refrigerator and did not rust. Technical improvements followed, including the ring pull, which removed the need for a can opener, and later the tab that stays attached to the can to reduce litter. Within thirty years aluminium had taken the majority of the market in the United States, and today it dominates the trade in canned drinks in most of the world.

G  The metal's environmental record is mixed. Extracting the oxide from bauxite leaves behind a toxic red sludge, and smelting still consumes vast amounts of electricity, much of it generated from fossil fuels. Yet aluminium has a redeeming quality: it can be melted down and reused again and again without losing its properties. Recycling it takes only about five per cent of the energy needed to make new metal from ore, which is why roughly three-quarters of all the aluminium ever produced is believed to be still in use. The can that was once the symbol of a throwaway society may, ironically, be one of the most recycled products in the world. A metal that was once reserved for emperors now sits in the recycling bin, and that is where its real value lies.

passages.title: How the eye evolved
paras: A  When Charles Darwin set out the theory of evolution by natural selection, he admitted that the eye caused him particular unease. To suppose that such a complex organ, with its adjustable focus, its control over the amount of light admitted and its correction of optical errors, could have arisen through gradual change seemed to him absurd in the highest degree. Yet he went on to argue that it was not absurd at all, provided that every small step along the way gave its owner some advantage. Modern research has largely vindicated him, and has added a surprising detail: eyes did not evolve once, but dozens of times, independently, in different branches of the animal kingdom.

B  The story starts with light-sensitive proteins. Many single-celled organisms contain pigment spots that cannot form images but can tell light from dark, which is enough for a cell to swim towards a sunlit surface where it can feed. The proteins involved, called opsins, are found in nearly all animals with eyes, from jellyfish to humans, which suggests that they were already in use in a common ancestor that lived well over 600 million years ago. The first true eyes were probably nothing more than a patch of such cells on the body surface, able to register changes in brightness but not to say where the light was coming from.

C  A flat patch can detect brightness but not direction. A slight dip in the surface changes that, since the walls of the pit shade some of the cells depending on where the light comes from. Deepening the pit into a cup sharpens this sense of direction, and narrowing the opening produces what is in effect a pinhole camera: light entering through a small aperture forms a crude image on the cells at the back. Some living animals show just this stage. The nautilus, a distant relative of the squid, has a pinhole eye with no lens, and sees a dim and fuzzy world. Yet each stage is useful in its own right, because even a poor image can warn an animal of the shadow of a predator.

D  The next step was the lens. A pinhole eye faces a trade-off: the smaller the opening, the sharper the image but the less light gets in. A transparent covering over the opening, which may at first have served only to protect the cavity from damage or infection, could also gather and focus light, so that the opening could be widened without blurring the picture. Two Swedish biologists once built a mathematical model in which a flat patch of cells was allowed to change by only one per cent at a time, and each change was kept only if it improved vision. Their model produced a camera-type eye with a lens in fewer than 400,000 generations, a mere blink in geological time.

E  Insects and crustaceans took a different route. Compound eyes are made up of hundreds or even thousands of separate units, each with its own tiny lens and each pointing in a slightly different direction. They give a coarse image but are superb at detecting movement, which explains why a fly is so hard to swat. The oldest compound eyes known belonged to trilobites, armoured sea creatures that disappeared long ago. Their lenses were made of calcite, the mineral of which limestone is composed, so these animals saw the world through crystal. The fossils show that sophisticated eyes existed more than 500 million years ago.

F  Why did eyes become so sophisticated so quickly? One controversial answer, sometimes called the light-switch hypothesis, proposes that the arrival of the first effective eyes triggered the burst of new animal forms in the Cambrian period, about 540 million years ago. Once predators could see their prey, it argues, prey evolved armour, speed and camouflage in response, and an arms race began. Critics point out that the evidence for eyes before the Cambrian is scarce, since soft tissue rarely fossilises, so the hypothesis cannot be tested directly. Many biologists prefer to see eyes as one contributor among several, together with rising oxygen levels and changes in ocean chemistry.

G  A comparison of the eyes of different animals shows that evolution does not always find the best design. The vertebrate eye, which includes our own, is wired back to front: light must pass through layers of nerve fibres and blood vessels before it reaches the photoreceptors, and the nerves gather at one spot to leave the eye, producing a blind spot. The eye of the octopus, which evolved independently and looks superficially similar, has its photoreceptors facing the light and no blind spot at all. It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that our design is poor. Having the blood supply behind the photoreceptors may help to feed these exceptionally hungry cells.

H  Some eyes are remarkable by any standard. The mantis shrimp has up to sixteen types of photoreceptor, compared with three in humans, although experiments suggest that this does not make it better at telling similar colours apart. Perhaps the most surprising discovery of all, though, concerns a gene called Pax6. This one gene acts as a master switch for eye development in animals as different as mice and fruit flies. When researchers activated it in the leg of a fruit fly, the leg grew an eye. Such findings suggest that, however varied eyes may be, they all draw on a shared genetic toolkit that is hundreds of millions of years old.

passages.title: Is nostalgia good for us?
paras: A  In 1688 a young Swiss medical student, Johannes Hofer, coined the word nostalgia from Greek roots meaning homecoming and pain. He used it to describe a condition afflicting Swiss mercenaries serving far from their mountain villages, whose symptoms included fever, loss of appetite and, in the worst cases, death. For the next two centuries doctors treated nostalgia as a disease, and in the twentieth century it was reclassified as a psychiatric disorder, a close relative of depression. Today most psychologists see it as a normal and even healthy emotion. I believe that this reversal is largely justified, although it has been celebrated with less caution than the evidence allows.

B  The case for rehabilitation rests on a body of experiments carried out over the past two decades. In one well-known series, Dr Helena Marsden asked volunteers to recall either a nostalgic event, such as a family holiday or a school concert, or an ordinary one, such as last Tuesday's shopping trip. Those who dwelt on the nostalgic memory reported better moods, felt more optimistic about the future and said they felt closer to other people. These results have been repeated by other laboratories many times, and I regard them as robust. Anyone who still thinks of nostalgia as a symptom of weakness should read this literature, which has grown steadily since the early years of the century and now runs to hundreds of published studies.

C  Professor Kofi Adjei offers an explanation of why this happens. In his view, the main benefit of nostalgia is not pleasure but meaning: remembering a birthday party or a favourite teacher reminds us that we have mattered to other people and that our lives form a story rather than a series of accidents. This would explain why loneliness, and the sense of purposelessness that goes with it, make people more likely to reach for nostalgic memories. Adjei's argument is persuasive, but it leans on studies of university students in Western countries, so the claim that nostalgia works in the same way everywhere has yet to be proved.

D  Not everyone is so positive. Dr Rafael Quintero warns of what he calls rosy retrospection, the habit of remembering the past as better than it really was by quietly deleting its boredom, discomfort and unfairness. His worry is that people who dwell on a golden past may become reluctant to tackle the problems of the present, since nothing today can match what they remember. It is a fair worry in principle. Yet the evidence he offers, a single study of forty adults who were asked to keep diaries, is thin, and I would not put much weight on it until it has been repeated with larger groups.

E  A separate concern is that nostalgia can be exploited. Marketers know that a person in a nostalgic mood is more willing to spend money, which is why old songs turn up in advertisements and old toys are relaunched as collectables. That is irritating but fairly harmless. Far more troubling is political nostalgia, in which leaders promise to restore a golden age that never existed and invite voters to blame outsiders for its disappearance. Because it deliberately distorts memory in order to win power, I consider this the more serious misuse. It would be wrong, however, to blame nostalgia itself for what is done in its name; a knife is not to blame for the crimes of the person who holds it.

F  A more useful line of research comes from Dr Ingrid Solberg, who distinguishes between passive and active nostalgia. Passive nostalgia is simply wishing that the past would return. Active nostalgia means using good memories as a source of ideas and energy, for instance by restarting a hobby abandoned years ago or reconnecting with a friend. In her studies of adults aged between thirty and seventy, only the active form was associated with greater wellbeing. I find this distinction the most helpful in the whole debate, because it shifts attention from the feeling itself to what we do with it. A memory that sends us back to the piano is a very different thing from one that keeps us on the sofa.

G  So is nostalgia good for us? On balance, I think it is, provided that certain conditions are met. We should enjoy it and share it, but not allow it to make our decisions for us or to take the place of plans for the future. We should also remain sceptical of anyone who tries to sell us the past, whether as a product or as a political programme. Rather than asking whether nostalgia is good or bad, we would do better to ask how it is used. The answer to that question, far more than the feeling itself, will decide whether looking back leaves us stronger or merely stuck.
